OIIX.name: FIR Tehran
OIIX.conflictType: Interstate conflict — Iran vs Israel/US (fragile ceasefire)
OIIX.narrative: EASA's CZIB-2026-04 reflects a ceasefire that has held since April 2026 but remains fragile, with an elevated Iranian air-defence posture that raises the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified. EASA has warned escalation could resume with little notice. The eastern part of the FIR was partially reopened for overflights in June 2026 while the western part remained closed; EASA's CZIB nonetheless continues to advise against operations at any altitude. The primary risk is misidentification of civil aircraft by air-defence systems during periods of heightened tension — a risk illustrated by Iran's shoot-down of Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran in Jan 2020. Most Europe-Asia traffic continues to route south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. OIIX/Tehran FIR remains only partially open; very few international operators are using it. Several states continue to warn against operations, and EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate at any altitude. Major events: July 2026: EASA CZIB continues — do not operate at any altitude. June 2026: Eastern OIIX partially reopened; western part remains closed. March 2026: FIR closed following large-scale US and Israeli strikes and subsequent Iranian missile/drone retaliation. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed warnings. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out mutual missile attacks; most operators avoided both airspaces. Jan 2020: Iran shot down Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran after misidentifying it as a hostile target.

ORBB.name: FIR Baghdad
ORBB.conflictType: Non-state armed groups (IBMGs) + Iranian missile/drone spillover
ORBB.narrative: Despite the regional ceasefire, EASA cites recurrent Iranian drone and ballistic-missile strikes reaching Iraqi airspace, alongside the continued presence of Iranian-backed militant groups (IBMGs), as reasons the Baghdad FIR remains a do-not-operate zone. The FIR reopened to overflights in June 2026 following the US-Iran ceasefire, with north-south routes available, but EASA's CZIB continues to advise against all operations. The primary risks are missile and drone activity linked to regional conflicts, misidentification by air-defence systems operated by local and foreign military forces, and an ongoing terrorist threat from groups possessing portable anti-aircraft weapons.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. ORBB/Baghdad FIR remains open to overflights and some operators continue using it; most Europe-Asia traffic still routes south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate at any altitude. Major events: July 2026: EASA CZIB continues — do not operate at any altitude. June 2026: FIR reopened following the US-Iran ceasefire; north-south routes available. March 2026: FIR closed following US/Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation. June 2025: Airspace closed following Israeli missile attack on Iran; missiles and drones transited Iraqi airspace. Apr 2024: Airspace closed due to Iran drone and missile strike on Israel. Apr 2023: Drone and missile attacks in northern Iraq from Turkey and Iran, including strikes near ORSU and ORER. Oct 2021: US operators permitted to overfly ORBB above FL320 under updated FAA restrictions.

OLBB.name: FIR Beirut
OLBB.narrative: A Trilateral Framework Agreement between Israel, Lebanon and the US (26 June 2026) is a step toward consolidating the ceasefire, but EASA notes its long-term implementation is uncertain, and that Lebanon has not shown it can proactively manage airspace risk. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon have continued despite repeated ceasefire extensions, and the primary risks remain military activity linked to the Israel-Hezbollah conflict, including missile and drone activity, and GNSS spoofing and jamming reported from Nov 2023 onwards. Some states allow limited operations to OLBA/Beirut provided arrivals and departures remain over the Mediterranean Sea.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon continue; most international operators avoid the airspace. Several states maintain long-standing warnings, and EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate at any altitude. Major events: July 2026: EASA CZIB continues — do not operate at any altitude. Feb-Jul 2026: Israeli airstrikes continued despite repeated ceasefire extensions. Oct 2024: Israel launched a ground operation against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon. Nov 2023 - ongoing: GNSS spoofing and jamming reported in the OLBB/Beirut FIR.

OJAC.name: FIR Amman
OJAC.conflictType: Missile/drone overflight risk (regional spillover, no direct conflict on Jordanian soil)
OJAC.narrative: Jordan's airspace has repeatedly seen Iranian missiles and drones pass through en route to other targets, intercepted by Jordanian and allied air defences. Jordanian authorities have not published any airspace restrictions of their own despite this activity. EASA has issued an Information Note advising operators to take the potential risk into account. The FIR remained open throughout the Iran conflict, and Jordan temporarily closed its airspace during the Iranian drone and missile attack on Israel in Apr 2024.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. OJAC/Amman FIR remains open and operating normally. EASA's current Information Note advises operators to take the potential risk into account. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new Information Note following renewed military activity in the Gulf. Feb-Jul 2026: Jordan remained open throughout the Iran conflict, although missile and drone activity affected several neighbouring countries. Apr 2024: Jordan temporarily closed its airspace during the Iranian drone and missile attack on Israel. Oct 2023: Jordan intercepted drones and missiles transiting its airspace during regional escalation.

OKAC.name: FIR Kuwait
OKAC.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OKAC.narrative: Kuwait hosts major US military facilities, making it a plausible target for Iranian retaliation and increasing the risk of civil aircraft being caught up in an attack or an air-defence response. Kuwait has been directly affected by the conflict, including missile and drone strikes that damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport in March 2026. The FIR is currently open for arrivals and departures only; overflights remain prohibited.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. OKAC/Kuwait FIR remains open for arrivals and departures only — overflights continue to be prohibited. EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate at any altitude. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate at any altitude. Feb-Jul 2026: OKAC/Kuwait FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict; currently open for arrivals/departures only. March 2026: Missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes across the region.

OBBB.name: FIR Bahrain
OBBB.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OBBB.narrative: As with Kuwait and Qatar, the US military presence in Bahrain is the main driver of EASA's risk assessment for this FIR. The FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before returning to normal overflight operations; Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted several Gulf states in March 2026, with incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. OBBB/Bahrain FIR remains open to overflights. EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate at any altitude. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate at any altitude. Feb-Jul 2026: OBBB/Bahrain FIR closed and reopened several times before returning to normal overflight operations. March 2026: Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted several Gulf states, with incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region.

OTDF.name: FIR Doha
OTDF.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OTDF.narrative: Qatar hosts significant US forces and has itself been targeted by Iranian strikes during the recent escalation, keeping it on EASA's do-not-operate list even as operational conditions ease. A missile strike was reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha in March 2026. The FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before returning to largely normal operations.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. OTDF/Doha FIR remains open and operating largely normally. EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate at any altitude. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate at any altitude. Feb-Jul 2026: OTDF/Doha FIR closed and reopened several times before returning to largely normal operations. March 2026: Iranian missile strike reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region.

OMAE.name: FIR Emirates
OMAE.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OMAE.narrative: The UAE's proximity to the Strait of Hormuz and its role as a regional hub keep it firmly within EASA's risk assessment, despite being operationally busy.

OOMM.name: FIR Muscat — west of 58°E only
OOMM.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OOMM.narrative: Unlike other Gulf FIRs, only the western portion of Omani/Gulf of Oman waters is covered — reflecting where commercial vessel attacks and Strait of Hormuz tension actually concentrate. Oman remained open throughout the Iran conflict and became a key part of the main southern bypass route (Egypt-Saudi-Oman) carrying significant Europe-Asia overflight traffic. EASA's CZIB advises against operations over the Gulf of Oman waters within the FIR west of 58°E.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. OOMM/Muscat FIR remains open and is a key part of the main southern bypass route. EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB covering Gulf of Oman waters west of 58°E. Feb-Jul 2026: Oman remained open throughout the Iran conflict and became a key part of the main southern bypass route. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed warnings across the Gulf. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out mutual missile attacks, leading many operators to avoid airspace between the two countries.

OSTT.name: FIR Damascus
OSTT.narrative: EASA's longest-running Middle East bulletin (19 revisions since 2017) reflects a still-unresolved multi-actor conflict. Traffic patterns have shifted: OSTT quietly reopened to some regional carriers in early 2025 as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq corridor, even though most Western operators continue to avoid it. The FIR was closed in March 2026 following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent regional retaliation, then saw a gradual increase in overflights from Jan–Jul 2026 as some operators used it as an alternative to Iran and Iraq. The primary risks are Israeli airstrikes targeting Iranian and Hezbollah-linked positions and the potential for misidentification by air-defence systems.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. OSTT/Damascus FIR remains high risk; some regional operators have started using it as an alternative to the Iran/Iraq routing. Several countries continue to prohibit or advise against operations due to military activity, anti-aviation weaponry and unstable security conditions. Major events: March 2026: FIR closed following US/Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent regional retaliation. Jan-Jul 2026: Gradual increase in overflights as some regional operators use the FIR as an alternative to Iran and Iraq. Dec 2024: Syrian airspace temporarily closed following the fall of the Assad regime. Oct 2023: Airstrikes damaged runways at OSDI/Damascus and OSAP/Aleppo airports. Feb 2020: An A320 approaching Damascus diverted after being caught in crossfire during Israeli airstrikes. Sep 2018: Russian IL-20 shot down in error near the Syria-Cyprus FIR boundary.

OYSC.name: FIR Sana'a only
OYSC.conflictType: Civil war + interstate spillover (Red Sea attacks)
OYSC.narrative: This bulletin covers only the Sana'a FIR, not the whole of Yemen. The ongoing civil war and Houthi involvement in the wider regional conflict keep the risk assessment unchanged since 2017. Several countries prohibit overflights of any land portion of the FIR; US operators may use offshore routes UT702 and M999, and some others permit flights on overwater portions. OYSN/Sanaa Airport has been closed since Dec 2024 due to damage from Israeli airstrikes.

cross.detail: OYSC/Sanaa FIR should be avoided. Several countries prohibit overflights of any land portion; US operators can use offshore routes UT702 and M999. The primary risks are intentional targeting by terrorist groups with sophisticated anti-aircraft weaponry and ongoing high-intensity military operations including explosive drones and missiles. Saudi and Israeli airstrikes can occur at any time, including in the capital Sana'a. Major events: Jul 2026: Yemen's government carried out an airstrike on the runway at OYSN/Sanaa Airport to stop an Iranian aircraft from landing. Dec 2024 - ongoing: OYSN/Sanaa Airport closed due to damage from Israeli airstrikes in Dec 2024 and May 2025. Jan 2024: US and UK carried out airstrikes against Houthi rebels in response to Red Sea missile and drone attacks. Sep 2023: Houthi drone attacks near the Yemen-Saudi border. Apr-Oct 2022: All parties agreed a ceasefire. 2018-2022: Frequent Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa and other targets in retaliation for Houthi drone attacks. 2017: OYSN/Sanaa Airport badly damaged by coalition airstrikes.

UUWV.name: FIR Moscow and others (west of 60°E)
UUWV.conflictType: Interstate war — Russian invasion of Ukraine (air-defence risk)
UUWV.narrative: Issued after the likely accidental shoot-down of Azerbaijan Airlines flight 8243 near Grozny in December 2024, this bulletin reflects the risk that Russian air-defence systems responding to Ukrainian strikes pose to civil aircraft, compounded by widespread GNSS interference. Drone attacks across Russia have continued to escalate, with some reaching as far as Siberia; hundreds of drones have been intercepted near Moscow using surface-to-air missiles capable of reaching all altitudes. Most activity occurs at night, but daytime disruptions are now common.

cross.detail: Drone attacks across Russia are escalating, including areas around Moscow, with Russian air-defence surface-to-air missiles capable of reaching all altitudes. Ukraine's airspace has remained fully closed since Feb 2022. Several countries prohibit operations in Russian airspace near FIR boundaries with Ukraine. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft through misidentification (cf. MAS17, UIA752). Major events: Jan 2025: EASA issued a new CZIB recommending against flights in western Russia (west of 60°E) due to anti-aircraft fire risk and high danger of misidentification, following the shoot-down of a passenger jet at URMG/Grozny on Dec 25. Jan 2024: Crash of military transport aircraft near Belgorod, approx 20nm from the Ukrainian border; both Russia and Ukraine accused each other of shooting it down. Aug 2023: Private jet carrying Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin crashed en route from Moscow to St Petersburg on Aug 23; speculation of a bomb onboard. July 2023 - ongoing: Drone strikes on Moscow and surroundings; some drones have damaged buildings, forcing temporary airport closures. Activity is becoming more frequent.

UKBV.name: All Ukrainian FIRs
UKBV.narrative: In force since the day of the invasion, this remains one of the clearest and most stable prohibitions in this dataset — Ukraine itself has closed its FIRs to civil traffic by NOTAM. Russia, Belarus and Moldova have closed large sections of their own airspace near FIR boundaries with Ukraine. All major states (US, UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy) have issued total flight bans. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft through misidentification or confusion; a secondary risk is the potential loss of Ukrainian ATC services at short notice.

cross.detail: Ukraine closed its entire airspace to all civil traffic on Feb 24, 2022, due to a military invasion by Russia. Russia, Belarus and Moldova have closed large sections of airspace near their FIR boundaries with Ukraine. All major states have issued total flight bans. The primary risk is unintended targeting through misidentification (cf. MAS17, UIA752) or confusion; the secondary risk is potential loss of Ukrainian ATC at short notice (e.g. cyber attack). Prior to February 2022, two areas of concern existed: conflict in the far east (affecting UKDV/Dnipro FIR) and the disputed ATC/airspace authority over Crimea (UKFV/URFV/Simferopol FIR).

HSSS.name: FIR Khartoum
HSSS.conflictType: Civil war — Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) vs Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
HSSS.narrative: The ongoing SAF–RSF civil war has put anti-aircraft artillery, MANPADS and SAM systems into play across the whole of Sudanese airspace, keeping the entire Khartoum FIR off-limits. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed and NOTAMs are not being issued; a contingency plan with published overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan is available. The primary risk on the ground is civil aircraft being targeted by gunfire at Khartoum airport; a secondary risk is Sudan's proximity to South Sudan, where ATC provision for overflights below FL245 is poor.

cross.detail: Sudan remains closed to all civilian flights following the April 2023 military coup, with ongoing fighting between government and militant forces. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed; no NOTAMs are being issued. A contingency plan with overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan is available. Several countries advise operators not to enter Sudanese airspace due to anti-aircraft weaponry and military activity risks. Major events: Nov 2025: Il-76 reportedly shot down by a surface-to-air missile near Babanusa, southern Sudan. May 2025: Drone attack targeting critical infrastructure including HSPN/Port Sudan airport. Oct 2024: Foreign-registered cargo aircraft shot down by local militia over North Darfur, near the border with Chad. Apr 2023: Military coup on Apr 15; Sudan's airspace closed, South Sudan's airspace closed above FL245. Oct 2021: Military coup on Oct 25; HSSK/Khartoum airport closed for two days with all flights suspended.

HLLL.name: FIR Tripoli
HLLL.narrative: Libya's two rival governments and various non-state armed actors create a real risk of misidentification when crossing between areas controlled by different authorities. The one carve-out is for coastal airport approaches made from over the sea. Reliable ATC services cannot be guaranteed: the past several years have seen regular ATS and radar outages across the FIR, severe VHF limitations, and militia threats to shoot down aircraft operating in western Libya including at HLLM/Mitiga airport.
HLLL.restrictionLabel: Do not operate, except flights to coastal airports approached from the sea, subject to ATC contact and your own risk assessment

cross.detail: Civil war ongoing since 2014; Libya remains an active conflict zone with armed clashes between rival militia groups. HLLL/Tripoli FIR should be avoided entirely. Total flight ban for US operators; several other countries have warnings in place. The primary risk is misidentification by Libyan air-defence systems or militia who have threatened to shoot down aircraft in western Libya, including at HLLM/Tripoli Mitiga airport. Military activity over the high seas operates as OAT or outside ATC control. The secondary risk is unreliable ATC, with regular ATS/radar outages and VHF limitations requiring operators to contact Malta ATC for guidance. Major events: August 2023: Major evacuation of aircraft from Tripoli due to violent clashes and gunfire at Mitiga airport. July 2023: Italy cancelled its 10-year ban on flights to/from Libya. Aug 2022: Militia air-defence forces claimed to have shot down a US drone near Benghazi. June 2022: Failed militia attempt to seize government offices in Tripoli; armed clashes and suspension of flights at HLLM/Mitiga. Jan 2020: Multiple airstrikes targeting HLLM/Mitiga airport. Nov 2019: Militia advancing on Tripoli declared a no-fly-zone, threatening to shoot down civil aircraft at HLLM/Mitiga. 2014: HLLT/Tripoli airport closed after militia clashes destroyed most facilities; most flights now operate from HLLM/Mitiga.

DRRR.name: Malian territory, especially the north-east
DRRR.conflictType: Insurgency — non-state armed groups active across the Sahel
DRRR.narrative: Non-state armed groups operating in Mali, particularly in the north-east, are assessed to have MANPADS and SAM missile capability, which is why the restriction is altitude-based rather than a total ban. ATS in Mali is provided by the GOOO/Dakar and DRRR/Niamey FIRs, which carry a long-standing restriction for overflights of Mali to published ATS routes at FL320 and above. The situation escalated sharply in April 2026, with coordinated attacks nationwide and sporadic fighting near GABS/Bamako.

cross.detail: Conflict in northern and central Mali ongoing since 2012; security situation remains volatile. Several countries advise operations at or above FL250 or FL260, avoiding GATB/Timbuktu, GAGO/Gao and GAKL/Kidal. The US advises caution at all levels due to expanding militant activity and a state-run paramilitary force operating anti-aircraft systems, military aircraft, UAS and electronic warfare equipment. Primary risks: MANPADS and surface-to-air weapons, indirect fire near airports, and misidentification risk. Low-level and airport-phase operations carry the highest exposure. ASECNA restricts Mali overflights to published ATS routes at FL320 and above. Major events: April 2026: Coordinated attacks nationwide on Apr 25 against state and military targets; gunfire and explosions near GABS/Bamako. France issued a new airspace warning advising against operations to/from GABS or its use as an alternate. Sep 2024: Insurgents breached GABS/Bamako and set the presidential jet on fire; multiple attacks across the city; airport temporarily closed. Dec 2023: Germany prohibited operations below FL260 in northern Mali; commercial flights to GATB/Timbuktu cancelled after shelling; a military jet crashed near GAGO/Gao, possibly shot down. Aug 2020: All airports closed for two days during a military coup; Bamako ACC remained operational and overflights were unaffected. Apr 2018: Militants attacked UN bases near GATB/Timbuktu with indirect fire and vehicle bombs. Jan 2017 and Nov 2016: Vehicle bomb and rocket attacks targeted GAGO/Gao and GATB/Timbuktu airports.

HCSM.name: Somali airspace
HCSM.conflictType: Insurgency — Al-Shabaab and related terrorist groups
HCSM.narrative: Terrorist organisations operating in Somalia are assessed to have confirmed anti-aircraft weaponry, possibly including MANPADS, driving the same FL260 altitude floor as Mali. A secondary risk arises from unauthorised ATC units issuing conflicting instructions to transiting aircraft. From Nov 2025, Somaliland has claimed all overflights require a PPR from its own CAA, while Somalia has reaffirmed through an AIC that it controls the entire FIR — expect conflicting permit instructions near Hargeisa and northern Somalia.

cross.detail: Highly unstable security situation; ongoing attacks by extremist militants targeting civilians, with continued intent to target aviation. The primary risk is anti-aircraft-capable weapons targeting overflying aircraft at lower flight levels. The US prohibits flights below FL260 except for overwater transits to/from HDAM/Djibouti. Several other countries advise against operating below FL260. The secondary risk is unauthorised ATC units issuing conflicting climb/descent instructions on official frequencies. From Nov 2025, Somaliland claims all overflights require a PPR from its own CAA; Somalia reaffirms through an AIC that it controls the entire FIR — expect conflicting permit instructions near Hargeisa and northern Somalia. Major events: Feb 2024: Multiple reports of aircraft being contacted by a 'fake controller' on the same frequency, issuing conflicting instructions. Aug 2023: Reports of uncontrolled combat helicopters operating at low levels (FL030) without position, altitude or routing reports. Oct 2022: Somalian government warned HCMM/Mogadishu airport may be targeted by militant groups. May 2022: Class A airspace implemented above FL245 in the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR. 2020-ongoing: Multiple Al-Shabaab attacks on HCMM/Mogadishu and nearby targets. May 2020: Embraer EMB-120 shot down on approach to Bardale airstrip, killing all six on board — accidental shoot-down by Ethiopian forces.

OPKR.name: Baluchistan province (partial)
OPKR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPKR.narrative: Violent non-state actor (VNSA) groups with confirmed MANPADS operate in Baluchistan. The Kashmir dispute separately raises misidentification risk further north. In May 2025 there were four days of cross-border strikes between India and Pakistan in Kashmir; the ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held but the situation remains fragile. Current guidance generally advises operators to remain at or above FL260.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. The May 2025 ceasefire has largely held but remains fragile. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions; current guidance advises at or above FL260. Primary risks: anti-aviation weaponry including MANPADS below FL260, and misidentification risk in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures; commercial traffic continues via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in Kashmir; ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held; some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan, highlighting cross-border military activity risk. Dec 2023 - ongoing: GPS spoofing reports in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in Kashmir.

OPLR.name: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province (partial)
OPLR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPLR.narrative: Covers the north-western province, where the Kashmir dispute adds a misidentification risk on top of the VNSA activity common to both restricted Pakistani provinces. GPS spoofing has been reported in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area from Dec 2023 onwards.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. The May 2025 ceasefire has largely held but remains fragile. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions; current guidance advises at or above FL260. Primary risks: anti-aviation weaponry including MANPADS below FL260, and misidentification risk in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures; commercial traffic continues via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in Kashmir; ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held; some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan, highlighting cross-border military activity risk. Dec 2023 - ongoing: GPS spoofing reports in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in Kashmir.

OAKX.name: FIR Kabul
OAKX.conflictType: Post-conflict security vacuum — extremist groups active, limited air traffic services
OAKX.narrative: Since the 2021 Taliban takeover, Afghanistan has had little to no functioning air traffic control. The Kabul FIR is Class G airspace: crews use published contingency routes and TIBA procedures rather than normal ATC clearances. Traffic increased through the FIR from March 2026 as flights used the northern bypass route around the closed Middle East corridor. Some countries restrict overflights to airways P500 and G500 in the far east of the FIR; others allow the entire airspace at or above FL320.

cross.detail: March 2026: OAKX/Kabul FIR remains open but has no ATC service; it is uncontrolled Class G airspace following the Aug 2021 withdrawal of US and allied forces. Traffic has increased as flights avoid the closed central Middle East corridor. Overflights must be on specific contingency routes; some countries restrict to airways P500 and G500 in the far east, others allow the entire FIR at or above FL320. Primary risks: surface-to-air fire at low altitudes, no ATC service, and extreme ground security threat. Major events: March 2026: Traffic increases through OAKX/Kabul FIR as flights use the northern bypass route. Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; commercial traffic continues via P500 and G500. Aug 2021: US and allied forces withdrew; OAKX/Kabul FIR became uncontrolled Class G airspace with no ATC service.

HAAA.name: FIR Addis Ababa, north of 8.5°N
HAAA.conflictType: Regional/border tension — assessed by EASA as medium risk
HAAA.narrative: This is an EASA Information Note, not a CZIB — meaning EASA's risk assessment group judged the risk here as medium rather than high. Full analytical detail is restricted to the CZ Hub. The risk picture in the northern Tigray region has improved since a peace deal in Nov 2022, but airspace warnings remain in place. A new flare-up of fighting in the Amhara region occurred in Feb 2024. The primary risk is large-scale ceasefire violations involving missiles or anti-aircraft weaponry that could endanger overflights.
HAAA.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: Improving risk picture in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region since the Nov 2022 peace deal, but airspace warnings remain. Primary risk: large-scale ceasefire violations involving missiles or anti-aircraft weaponry endangering overflights or causing misidentification. Major events: Feb 2024: New flare-up in the Amhara region (south of Tigray), including air strikes. Nov 2022: Peace deal agreed in Tigray; Ethiopian Airlines planning to resume flights to HAMK/Mekele. Nov 2021: Several western countries issued airspace warnings and 'do not travel' advisories for Tigray following increased fighting. July 2021: HAAA/Addis FIR NOTAM closed airspace below FL290 over Tigray following reports that militia shot down a military transport plane near Mekele. Nov 2020: Major escalation in Tigray; airways including UN321, UG300 and UL432 closed or threatened; rockets targeted airports; missiles fired into Eritrea targeting HHAS/Asmara; HABD/Bahir Dar and HAGN/Gondar also targeted. Sep 2018: Hidden ATC strike by Ethiopian controllers; ECAA and Ethiopian Airlines used retired and foreign controllers, some unqualified for Ethiopian airspace; strike ended Sep 7.

VYYF.name: FIR Yangon, below FL260
VYYF.conflictType: Internal armed conflict — assessed by EASA as medium risk
VYYF.narrative: As with Ethiopia, this is a medium-risk Information Note rather than a do-not-operate CZIB. France's own national guidance goes slightly further operationally, setting a hard altitude floor. The security situation has deteriorated since the Feb 2021 military coup, with air strikes and armed clashes across many parts of the country. GPS jamming has been reported on airway N895 and in the north of the FIR.
VYYF.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: Security situation in Myanmar has deteriorated since the Feb 2021 military coup, with conflict and air strikes across many parts of the country. Several countries advise against operating at lower flight levels due to military operations, surface-to-air fire and anti-aviation weaponry. GPS jamming (and possible spoofing) reported in the north of the FIR and on airway N895. Major events: Jan 2024: Armed group shot down a military helicopter in Kachin state using a likely MANPAD. Sep 2023: Rebel groups attacked military targets nationwide, including a makeshift drone bombing aircraft hangars at an airbase next to VYNT/Naypyitaw airport. Sep 2023: Intermittent GPS jamming reported on airway N895. Apr 2023: VYYY/Yangon temporarily closed following an improvised artillery attack by resistance groups. Sep 2022: A Myanmar National Airlines passenger reportedly shot as bullets passed through the fuselage of the ATR 72 on approach to VYLK/Loikaw. Feb 2021: Military coup ousted the government; ATC strike at end of Feb left no ATC service for overflights; increasing clashes with militia and airstrikes on militia-active areas have followed.
